transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brought you in to see me today?

I’ve been really preoccupied with a scar on my wrist. I know it probably looks worse to me than it does to other people, but at church or when I’m playing bridge, I feel like everyone notices it right away. Like it’s the first thing they see about me.
On an average day, about how many hours would you say you spend thinking about or worrying about that scar?
I’m not sure of the exact hours. It comes up a lot, especially if I’m at church or playing bridge—then I keep thinking people are looking right at my wrist.
Aside from worrying about your scar, do you also find yourself worrying a lot about other things in your life—like health, finances, or family—on most days?
Not really, no. Mostly it’s the scar that gets in my head.
Do you find yourself doing things like checking the scar in the mirror, trying to cover it up with clothing or makeup, or asking others if it looks noticeable?

Yes. Before I leave the house, I’ll check my wrist in the hall mirror a few times. I try different sleeves or wear a bracelet to cover it, and sometimes I ask my husband if it looks obvious. He always tells me it’s barely there.
When your husband tells you the scar is barely noticeable, do you believe he might be right, or do you feel certain that he's just being kind and it really does look as bad as you think?
I know he may be right—that it probably isn’t as bad as it looks to me. But at church or bridge, I still feel like everyone’s eyes go straight to my wrist, like it’s the first thing they notice.

latest_inference.note: Patient's acknowledgment that her husband may be right and the scar likely isn't as bad as she perceives supports fair/good insight, consistent with body dysmorphic disorder rather than a delusional variant. Repetitive checking, camouflaging (sleeves/bracelet), and reassurance-seeking further support this diagnosis, and absence of broader worry rules out generalized anxiety disorder.
